The attacker becomes a machine-in-the-middle: they can read and change every request and response, including session tokens and credentials sent to the backend, for any device where the flag is active.",

        "title": "Release builds must always validate TLS certificates",
        "given": "a release build of the mobile app",
        "when": "it connects to the backend and is presented with a certificate that is not trusted for that hostname",
        "then": "the connection is refused, and no configuration, flag or runtime setting can disable certificate or hostname validation in a release build"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Tampering",
      "title": "The insecure flag ships to production inside the release build and can be switched on",
      "scenario": "The flag that disables certificate checking is read from a config file bundled in the release build, so the unsafe code path exists on every customer device. Anyone who can edit that file - an attacker with device or filesystem access, a repackaged/sideloaded copy of the app, or a build-config mistake - turns off certificate validation for real users and then intercepts their traffic. No backend change is needed.",
      "component": "Bundled config file / environment flag reader",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The flag is read from a config file bundled in the release build." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-489", "CWE-15"],
      "plainLanguage": "The test-only switch is shipped to real users, so flipping a file in the app turns off security for them.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Insecure test behaviour must be compiled out of release builds",
        "given": "the certificate-bypass behaviour used for testing",
        "when": "a release artifact is built",
        "then": "the bypass code path is excluded at compile time (debug-only build variant), the bundled config cannot enable it, and CI fails the build if the bypass symbol or flag is present in the release artifact"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Intercepted traffic exposes session tokens and user data from the app",
      "scenario": "Because a bypassed certificate check lets an attacker terminate TLS themselves, all app-to-backend traffic is readable in clear text to them. They harvest bearer tokens, cookies or API keys from the captured requests and replay them against the backend from their own machine, acting as the user without ever needing the user's password.",
      "component": "App to backend API channel",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "To help testing, the app accepts any TLS certificate when the environment flag is set." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-319"],
      "plainLanguage": "If someone can read the app's traffic, they can steal the login token and pretend to be the user.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Protect app credentials against a machine-in-the-middle",
        "given": "a release build communicating with the backend",
        "when": "the TLS peer cannot be verified as the expected backend",
        "then": "no session token, credential or user data is transmitted, and the app surfaces a connection error instead of falling back to an unverified channel"
      }
    }
  ]
